chapters.title: Studio Management Scorecard
facts:
Margin is improving. Revenue attributed to attended classes rose from ₹9,81,453 to ₹13,06,451 on
14 fewer classes, and revenue per class rose from ₹3,595 to ₹5,044 . Revenue per attendance rose from ₹665 to ₹931. The average September buyer
spent ₹11,003 against ₹10,432 a year ago.

Discipline is improving. Late cancellations fell from 658 to 199, and the share of the board that was ever
booked at all fell from 60.5% to 48.7% — which sounds like bad news
and is, but it is honest news: the studio is no longer counting seats nobody intended to use.

Acquisition has stalled. Bandra created 189 leads in September 2026, against a 2026 monthly average of
211 and a 2025 average of 198. Of every lead the studio has ever recorded for this location, 12.9% became a member and 18.4% are retained today.

Frequency has never been managed. 327 memberships are live, worth ₹85,62,873 of recorded cash. 117 of those members, holding ₹23,65,012, have not been in the studio for fifteen days or more. No one is currently responsible for that list,
and it is the largest recoverable number in this report.

facts: Class performance is the one part of Bandra’s September that improved on nearly every measure, and it deserves to be said clearly before the problems. The studio ran 259 classes against 273 a year earlier — a leaner timetable — and filled 42.6% of the seats against 41.8% . Revenue attributed to attended classes rose from ₹9,81,453 to ₹13,06,451 , up 33%, making it the only revenue line in the studio that grew. Revenue per class rose 40% to ₹5,044; revenue per attendee rose from ₹665 to ₹931. Late cancellations fell from 658 to 199.
Every one of those is a genuine operational gain, and two Septembers of improvement in a row — from 27.3% in 2024 to 41.8% to 42.6% — is a trend rather than noise.

What the same numbers also show is a large and specific inefficiency that has been carried for three years without being addressed. The studio holds a fixed-cost timetable and fills just over two seats in five. In September 2026 it offered 3,293 seats and used 1,404 of them. The unused 1,889 seats are not evenly spread: they are concentrated in particular formats, particular days and particular hours, and the concentration is stable enough across two years to be treated as a design flaw rather than a bad month.

The single most useful sentence in this report is this: Studio PowerCycle runs 35% of the timetable and fills 35.0% of it, while Studio FIT runs 15% of the timetable and fills 71.0%. Both are good products with loyal followings. Only one of them is being given the right amount of the week.

chapters.title: Membership Health, Retention & Lapse
facts:
Every membership ever sold at Bandra sits in this ledger: 8,707 memberships taken out by 3,768 people , of which
3,974 were paid memberships from 1,699 members. Read forward from purchase, the pattern is stark and consistent across two years of
trading: one in five paid memberships ends within a week. More than half end within a month. Only 3.2% are still in force a year later.

The median paid Bandra membership lasts 19 days . Not months — days. And it has shortened: the median membership bought in 2024
ran 29 days, one bought in 2025 ran 17, and one bought so far in 2026 is running 19.
Every retention, referral and frequency conversation the studio has depends on that number, and it is getting worse.

The reassuring reading is in how people are lost rather than how many. Among memberships with enough visits to measure a trend, 37.2% ran a second half that was half the first or worse — and
10.5% ended with a second half in which the member did not attend at all. They did not cancel, complain or ask for a refund. They
drifted, while the membership was still live and still contactable. That is a recoverable failure, and it is what this report is built around.

At Bandra the derived statuses read: 7,745 lapsed (89.0%),
371 in a renewal grace period, 352 never activated,
111 active and 77 renewed.

chapters.title: Format Performance & Programming Strategy
facts:
September 2026 ran 259 classes across 12 formats , drew 1,404 attendances and attributed ₹13,06,451 of revenue to them. But the three largest formats are almost identical in scale and wildly different in behaviour. PowerCycle and Barre 57 together carry 55% of the timetable and fill
35.0% and 44.6% respectively. Studio FIT carries 15% and fills 71.0%.

The reason this is not simply a scheduling problem is visible in the member data. PowerCycle reaches 181 distinct members in the month — more than any other format — while FIT reaches 104. But of FIT’s members, 23.1% came four or more times inside the month . Of PowerCycle’s, 17.1% did.
FIT is not a bigger product. It is a stickier one, and the studio is giving the stickier product less than half the week.

Set the formats side by side and a division of labour emerges that the studio is not currently managing deliberately. FIT wins on fill (71.0%),
revenue per class (₹6,999) and regularity (23.1%). Mat 57 is second on fill at
55.1% on a small timetable. PowerCycle leads on absolute attendance simply because it runs 90 sessions.
And the express formats — PowerCycle X at 52.6%, Cardio Barre X at 15.3% —
are the widest spread in the table, which tells the studio that format length matters more than format family.

Read on revenue per head, however, the differences almost vanish: ₹858 to ₹1,142 , a spread of
33%. That is a striking result. It means the audience is worth roughly the same per person wherever they sit. Formats do not differ in the value of the member. They differ in how many members the studio can get into the room.

chapters.title: Revenue & Capacity Leakage
facts:
Start with the good news, because it is real and it is measurable. Across every seat booked at Bandra this year, 86.3% were attended and only
12.9% became a late cancellation . In 2025 those figures were 72.8% and 27.1%; in 2024, 80.4% and
19.2%. Late cancellations fell from 6,660 seats in 2025 to 2,064 this year , while the number of attending visits rose.
Whatever changed in how the studio communicates expections around bookings, it worked.

In September 2026 specifically, 199 seats were released late against 1,404 attendances. That is 14.2 late cancellations for every
hundred classes attended — a level the studio can live with, and one it can reduce further.

The discount story moves the other way. The studio discounted ₹19,99,121 in 2026 so far, at a depth of 10.7% of gross , against
8.0% in 2024. Discount spread has fallen — fewer sales carry an offer — but the offers that are made are deeper, and they are concentrated
on the products that needed them least. That is the finding worth acting on.

The value of a released seat is not fixed. It is worth almost nothing in a half-empty room and a great deal in a full one. In September the board ran at 48.7% occupancy on the booking book when those 199 seats were released, against 60.5% in September 2025.
More than half the seats were unsold at the moment they were given back.

chapters.title: Lead Funnel & Acquisition Health
facts: Read the whole file and three things stand out above everything else.

First, the trial decides everything. 3,493 of 7,822 leads completed a trial; 911 of them bought. Of the 4,329 who never took a trial, 95 ever bought anything . The trial is not a step in the funnel — it is the funnel.

Second, the sale happens the day the enquiry arrives. 61% of every membership Bandra sells is sold on the same day ,
and the median lead buys on the day it enquires. Everything after that is a small, slow tail.

Third, the studio’s biggest channel is its weakest. Website and online sources deliver 3,714 leads — 47% of the file —
and convert 8.9% of them at ₹4,120 of lifetime value. Calls, messages and referrals together deliver 1,920 leads and convert
23.9% of them at ₹9,031.

chapters.title: Member Engagement & Attendance Behaviour
facts:
The studio’s members are morning people. 249 of 394 members do most of their training before noon, against 129 who come in the evening.
The busiest hours of September were 11:00 (265 check-ins) and 09:00 (252), and the busiest day was Tuesday.

They come in clusters, not on a schedule. The median gap between a member’s visits is 1 day , and 85% of every gap on record is a
week or less. Bandra members do not train twice a week; they come three days running and then not for a fortnight.

And the loss is concentrated in one step. Across 1,785 first-timers, 40.5% make a second visit, and of those 70% go on to a third .
59.5 points of the cohort are lost at the first repeat visit — and then the curve reverses: from the second visit onward, each next visit is more likely than the last.

This studio does not leak members steadily. It loses most of them once, in their first fortnight, and it never sees the moment coming because it measures attendance rather than the interval between visits.

facts: The most important fact about September 2026 is what it is not . It is not the month the studio's fundamentals broke. Over the twelve months to September, Bandra's second-visit rate held at 29.2% versus 29.1% the year before , and the revenue generated per new client within 90 days rose to ₹2,431 from ₹2,259 — the second consecutive annual improvement. Volume across the trailing twelve months was effectively flat, at 1,439 clients against 1,475.

Year-to-date the picture is equally reassuring on the metric that matters most. Across January to September 2026, the share of new clients who returned for a second class was 39.1%, against 39.2% in 2025 and 37.4% in 2024. Whatever went wrong in September, it did not go wrong for the year.

One qualification belongs here rather than in a footnote, because it cuts across every retention figure in this report and is quantified in full later. Roughly a third of what the studio records as a "second visit" is the pre-paid second half of a Newcomers 2 For 1 intro pack — a class the client has already bought and is simply using up. These year-level rates are therefore the right measure for spotting change over time, because the same distortion runs through all three years, but they overstate the absolute level of genuine repeat demand. Where a true return rate is quoted below, the pre-paid visits have been removed.

What September did was concentrate a set of already-visible weaknesses into a single month, in a way that is now measurable and therefore fixable. This edition adds three further sources — the full 150,895-row check-in ledger, the 25,315-record lead register and the 25,044-record sales ledger — which together make it possible to say not just what happened in September but where it happened and who it happened to.
